notes.front: In the tool standards, what is the point of operation?
notes.back: The area on a machine where work is actually performed on the material being processed.
notes.explanation: It is where the tool meets the material, and 1926.300 requires it to be guarded where its operation exposes an employee to injury.
notes.example: Like the spot where a saw blade bites into a board, as opposed to the motor housing or the belt drive.
notes.evidence: Point of operation is the area on a machine where work is actually performed upon the material being processed.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(b)(4)(i), Point of operation guarding, p. 202

notes.front: Which hand and power tools must be maintained in a safe condition?
notes.back: All of them, whether furnished by the employer or by the employee.
notes.explanation: Ownership does not matter: a worker's own tool on site is covered as much as the company's.
notes.evidence: All hand and power tools and similar equipment, whether furnished by the employer or the employee, shall be maintained in a safe condition.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(a), Condition of tools, p. 201

notes.front: A carpenter brings his own circular saw with a cracked housing. The foreman says the rule only covers company tools. Is he right?
notes.back: B: no; tools must be kept safe whether furnished by the employer or the employee.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, employee-owned tools are the employee's business
B) No; tools must be kept safe whether furnished by the employer or the employee
C) Yes, if the carpenter signs a waiver
D) No, but only if the saw is used indoors
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: the rule covers employee-furnished tools and allows no waiver. D adds a condition the rule does not have.
notes.explanation: The rule covers tools and equipment furnished by either party.
notes.evidence: All hand and power tools and similar equipment, whether furnished by the employer or the employee, shall be maintained in a safe condition.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(a), Condition of tools, p. 201

notes.front: When a power-operated tool is designed to accommodate guards, when must it have them?
notes.back: It must be equipped with such guards when in use.
notes.explanation: The design sets the expectation: if the tool was built to take a guard, it is used with one.
notes.evidence: guards, they shall be equipped with such guards when in use.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(b)(1), Guarding, p. 202

notes.front: Which moving parts of equipment must be guarded?
notes.back: Belts, gears, shafts, pulleys, chains and other reciprocating, rotating or moving parts exposed to contact or otherwise creating a hazard.
notes.explanation: The test is exposure to contact by employees, or another hazard the part creates.
notes.evidence: Belts, gears, shafts, pulleys, sprockets, spindles, drums, fly wheels, chains, or other reciprocating, rotating or moving parts of equipment shall be guarded if such parts are exposed to contact by employees or otherwise create a hazard.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(b)(2), Guarding, p. 202

notes.front: When must the point of operation of a machine be guarded, and what must the guard prevent?
notes.back: When operation exposes an employee to injury; it must keep any part of the operator's body out of the danger zone during the cycle.
notes.explanation: That design aim applies where no specific standard for the guarding device exists.
notes.evidence: whose operation exposes an employee to injury, shall be guarded. The guarding device shall be in conformity with any appropriate standards therefor, or, in the absence of applicable specific standards, shall be so designed and constructed as to prevent the operator from having any part of his body in the danger zone
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(b)(4)(ii), Point of operation guarding, p. 202

notes.front: A worker removes the lower blade guard from a portable saw designed to take one, because it slows his cuts. What does 1926.300 require?
notes.back: A: the saw must be used with its guard.
notes.choices:
A) The saw must be used with its guard
B) The guard may be removed for skilled operators
C) The guard may be removed if he wears PPE
D) Guards are optional on portable tools
notes.choicesExplained: B and D invent exceptions. C is wrong: PPE does not replace a guard the tool was designed to take.
notes.explanation: A tool designed to accommodate guards must be equipped with them when in use.
notes.evidence: guards, they shall be equipped with such guards when in use.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(b)(1), Guarding, p. 202

notes.front: What kind of switch must hand-held circular saws and chain saws have?
notes.back: A constant pressure switch that shuts off the power when the pressure is released.
notes.explanation: The rule covers hand-held powered tools such as these that are not in the lists allowed simpler switches.
notes.evidence: All other hand-held powered tools, such as circular saws, chain saws, and percussion tools without positive accessory holding means, shall be equipped with a constant pressure switch that will shut off the power when the pressure is released.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(d)(3), Switches, p. 203

notes.front: Which kind of control may hand-held jigsaws with blade shanks a quarter inch wide or less have?
notes.back: A positive "on-off" control on its own is permitted.
notes.explanation: The same allowance covers other small tools listed, such as routers and grinders with wheels 2 inches or less.
notes.evidence: and jigsaws with blade shanks one-fourth of an inch wide or less may be equipped with only a positive ‘‘on-off’’ control.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.300, General requirements(d)(1), Switches, p. 203

notes.front: What does 1926.301 forbid employers to do with unsafe hand tools?
notes.back: Issue them, or permit their use.
notes.explanation: The duty covers permitting use as well as issuing, so it reaches tools the employer did not hand out.
notes.evidence: Employers shall not issue or permit the use of unsafe hand tools.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.301, Hand tools(a), p. 204

notes.front: When must a wrench not be used?
notes.back: When its jaws are sprung to the point that slippage occurs.
notes.explanation: The rule names adjustable, pipe, end and socket wrenches.
notes.evidence: Wrenches, including adjustable, pipe, end, and socket wrenches shall not be used when jaws are sprung to the point that slippage occurs.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.301, Hand tools(b), p. 204

notes.front: What must impact tools such as drift pins, wedges and chisels be kept free of?
notes.back: Mushroomed heads.
notes.explanation: The rule lists these three impact tools by name.
notes.evidence: Impact tools, such as drift pins, wedges, and chisels, shall be kept free of mushroomed heads.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.301, Hand tools(c), p. 204

notes.front: What condition must the wooden handles of tools be kept in?
notes.back: Free of splinters or cracks, and tight in the tool.
notes.explanation: A handle can fail by splitting or by working loose, and the rule covers both.
notes.evidence: The wooden handles of tools shall be kept free of splinters or cracks and shall be kept tight in the tool.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.301, Hand tools(d), p. 204

notes.front: On a morning check, a supervisor finds a cold chisel with a mushroomed head and a hammer with a cracked handle in the site toolbox. What should happen?
notes.back: C: they must not be issued or used until made safe or replaced.
notes.choices:
A) Use them until the end of the job
B) Tape the handle and carry on
C) They must not be issued or used until made safe or replaced
D) Use them only for light work
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D all permit the use of unsafe hand tools, which the rule forbids.
notes.explanation: Employers may not issue or permit the use of unsafe hand tools, and both defects are named in 1926.301.
notes.evidence: Employers shall not issue or permit the use of unsafe hand tools.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.301, Hand tools(a), p. 204

notes.front: How must electric power-operated tools be protected electrically?
notes.back: They must be of the approved double-insulated type, or grounded in accordance with Subpart K.
notes.explanation: Either route meets the rule; a tool that is neither does not.
notes.evidence: Electric power operated tools shall either be of the approved double-insulated type or grounded in accordance with subpart K of this part.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.302, Power-operated hand tools(a)(1), Electric power-operated tools, p. 204

notes.front: A drill is not double-insulated, and its earth pin has been snapped off the plug. What does 1926.302 require?
notes.back: C: it may not be used until grounded in accordance with Subpart K.
notes.choices:
A) It may be used on dry days
B) It may be used if held by the insulated grip
C) It may not be used until grounded in accordance with Subpart K
D) It may be used for short jobs only
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D leave a tool that is neither double-insulated nor grounded in use.
notes.explanation: A tool that is not approved double-insulated must be grounded under Subpart K.
notes.evidence: Electric power operated tools shall either be of the approved double-insulated type or grounded in accordance with subpart K of this part.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.302, Power-operated hand tools(a)(1), Electric power-operated tools, p. 204

notes.front: May an electric tool be raised or lowered by its cord?
notes.back: No: using electric cords for hoisting or lowering tools is not permitted.
notes.explanation: The pneumatic rules say the same of air hoses.
notes.evidence: The use of electric cords for hoisting or lowering tools shall not be permitted.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.302, Power-operated hand tools(a)(2), Electric power-operated tools, p. 204

notes.front: A worker on a scaffold asks his mate to send up a grinder by tying a knot in its cord. What should the mate do?
notes.back: D: use a hand line or other means; hoisting a tool by its electric cord is not permitted.
notes.choices:
A) Tie the knot tightly and lift
B) Unplug the tool first, then lift by the cord
C) Lift by the air hose instead
D) Use a hand line or other means; hoisting a tool by its electric cord is not permitted
notes.choicesExplained: A and B still hoist by the cord. C is wrong: hoses may not be used for hoisting or lowering tools either.
notes.explanation: The rule bars electric cords from being used to hoist or lower tools.
notes.evidence: The use of electric cords for hoisting or lowering tools shall not be permitted.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.302, Power-operated hand tools(a)(2), Electric power-operated tools, p. 204

notes.front: When must fuel-powered tools be stopped?
notes.back: While being refuelled, serviced or maintained.
notes.explanation: Fuel must also be transported, handled and stored under Subpart F.
notes.evidence: All fuel powered tools shall be stopped while being refueled, serviced, or maintained,
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.302, Power-operated hand tools(c)(1), Fuel powered tools, p. 204

notes.front: When may a powder-actuated tool be loaded, and may a loaded tool be left unattended?
notes.back: Only just prior to the intended firing time; a loaded tool must never be left unattended.
notes.explanation: Neither loaded nor empty tools may be pointed at anyone.
notes.evidence: (5) Tools shall not be loaded until just prior to the intended firing time. Neither loaded nor empty tools are to be pointed at any employees. Hands shall be kept clear of the open barrel end. (6) Loaded tools shall not be left unattended.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.302, Power-operated hand tools(e)(5)–(6), Powder-actuated tools, p. 205

notes.front: Who may operate a powder-actuated tool?
notes.back: Only employees trained in the operation of the particular tool in use.
notes.explanation: The training is tool-specific, and the tool must be tested each day before loading.
notes.evidence: Only employees who have been trained in the operation of the particular tool in use shall be allowed to operate a powderactuated tool. (2) The tool shall be tested each day before loading
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.302, Power-operated hand tools(e)(1)–(2), Powder-actuated tools, p. 204

notes.front: What must be done to abrasive wheels before mounting?
notes.back: Close inspection and a ring test, to ensure they are free from cracks or defects.
notes.explanation: Grinding wheels must also fit freely on the spindle and not be forced on.
notes.evidence: All abrasive wheels shall be closely inspected and ring-tested before mounting to ensure that they are free from cracks or defects.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.303(c)(7), Use of abrasive wheels, p. 206

notes.front: On a floor-stand or bench grinder, how much of the wheel periphery and sides may the safety guard leave exposed?
notes.back: Not more than 90°, or 125° where work must contact the wheel below the spindle's horizontal plane.
notes.explanation: Either way, the exposure must begin no more than 65° above the horizontal plane of the spindle.
notes.evidence: The maximum angular exposure of the grinding wheel periphery and sides shall be not more than 90°, except that when work requires contact with the wheel below the horizontal plane of the spindle, the angular exposure shall not exceed 125°.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.303(c)(1), Use of abrasive wheels, p. 205

notes.front: What must be marked on every jack, and what must never happen to that figure?
notes.back: The manufacturer's rated capacity, legibly marked; it shall not be exceeded.
notes.explanation: Every jack must also have a positive stop to prevent overtravel.
notes.evidence: The manufacturer’s rated capacity shall be legibly marked on all jacks and shall not be exceeded. (2) All jacks shall have a positive stop to prevent overtravel.
